C1.claim: Real fp32 and fp16 tiles with no exact zeros cost within 2% of random data of their format over its zeros, in every model

C2.claim: On average real fp32 and fp16 tiles with no exact zeros sit below random data of their format

C3a.claim: A ReLU tile's power follows its live share: each fp32 and fp16 ReLU tile lies inside the gate law's interval

C3b.claim: Across the ReLU tiles of a format, D rises with the live share at about the random kind's full cost

C4.claim: The same numbers cost more in fp16 than in fp32 because a zero must fill the whole 32-bit word

C5.claim: In int8 a real ReLU tile's power follows its operand bits more than its live share: the predictor (a) lies nearer the measurement than the gate law (c)

C6.claim: On a GELU layer with one huge activation the calibration is a lever several times larger than any data effect: 99.9th percentile clip against max-abs

C7.claim: On E86's window the calibrations rank committed < per-token < 99.9th percentile by power; the 99.99th percentile clip sits beside committed

C8.claim: TFLite-style asymmetric activations show the gate nothing on a ReLU tile, so the same numbers cost more than the symmetric tile

C9.claim: The gate tests word == 0, so -0.0 passes it: a tile whose A is 64% -0.0 (the layer: 55%) costs more than the gate law allows if the gate took numeric zeros

C10.claim: T5's weights sit on the bf16 grid (all low 16 mantissa bits zero), so a no-zero T5 tile costs clearly less than random fp32, unlike E86's full-mantissa tiles

C11.claim: An fp16 forward pass costs what rounding the fp32 activations costs
